candidates.abstract: Describes the headland, small harbour and quay of Ponta do Sol, on Madeira's south-west coast, and the possible origin of the name. The quay was built by the municipal council in 1848–1850; a later extension project of 1880 was never carried out.

candidates.abstract: Entry on the parish of Porto do Moniz on Madeira's north-west coast, one of the oldest northern parishes, founded around the estate and chapel of Francisco Moniz, the Elder. It covers the origin of its name, its churches and chapels, the fort built against corsairs, and its localities and population.

History of the municipality of Porto Moniz in north-western Madeira, created in 1835 after long local petitions, and repeatedly abolished and restored in the nineteenth century. Porto Moniz was never raised to the status of a vila, only serving as the seat of the concelho.

Describes the harbour of Porto do Moniz, reputedly the safest and most sheltered anchorage on Madeira's north coast, used as a refuge when southerly winds close the southern ports. It records hydrographic studies of 1914 and harbour works carried out between 1901 and 1916.

payload.name: Ilhéus
notes: [Diniz (Julio)] Area where he briefly lived in a house.

own_entry.abstract: A list of the main islets off the coasts of Madeira and Porto Santo, and in the Desertas group, each with the parish it lies near. It serves as an index to their individual entries.

payload.name: Ermida
notes: [Santo António da Serra (Freguesia de)] Locality named after the early chapel.

own_entry.abstract: Inhabited locality in Santo da Serra parish, Machico, named after a small hermitage built there by Gil de Carvalho in the second quarter of the 16th century.

payload.name: Aldeia da Rainha
notes: [Santo António da Serra (Freguesia de)] Name of the 1768 settlement.

own_entry.abstract: A short-lived settlement founded in the parish of Santo António da Serra in the reign of Queen Maria I, peopled by families from Porto Santo.

payload.name: Rua do Príncipe
notes: [Saúde (Rua da)] The other end of the present rua and calçada da Saúde.

own_entry.abstract: Former name of the Funchal street running alongside the Ribeira de Santa Luzia, from the Calçada do Cidrão to the Rua dos Netos, renamed Rua 5 de Outubro after the Republic was proclaimed. The name probably honoured the Prince Regent D. João VI, though no municipal record confirms it.

payload.name: Capela de Nossa Senhora da Saúde
notes: [Saúde (Rua da)] The chapel that gave the street its name.

own_entry.abstract: A chapel on Rua da Saúde, São Pedro, Funchal, founded in 1659 and no longer used for worship.

payload.name: Nossa Senhora da Graça
notes: [Profetas] Chapel to which the people processed at the prophets' order.

own_entry.abstract: Four chapels of Our Lady of Grace, in Porto Santo, Machico, Santa Cruz and Funchal's Sé parish; the octagonal Porto Santo chapel is notable and now ruined.

payload.name: Lombo de D. Isabel
notes: [Aviceiro ou Fonte do Aviceiro] Nearby locality a short distance from Aviceiro.

own_entry.abstract: Locality in Santo António parish, Funchal, bordering Vasco Gil and crossed by the road to Curral das Freiras.

payload.name: Lombo das Mercês
notes: [Lombo das Mercês] The locality described in this entry.

own_entry.abstract: A locality within the populated sítio of Florenças in the parish of Arco da Calheta, named after the entailed chapel of Nossa Senhora das Mercês founded in 1650. A chapel to Santa Maria Madalena is also said to have been built there in 1684.

payload.name: Capela de Nossa Senhora das Mercês
notes: [Lombo das Mercês] Entailed chapel founded in 1650 that gave the locality its name.

own_entry.abstract: Chapel of Our Lady of Mercy founded in 1650 at Florenças, Arco da Calheta.

payload.name: Lombo da Pereira
notes: [Lombo da Pereira] Locality where an orphanage for poor children was founded in 1922.

own_entry.abstract: Entry on the sítio of Lombo da Pereira in the parish of Santo da Serra, notable for the orphanage for poor children founded there by Padre José Lino da Costa and opened in 1922.

payload.name: Capela de Nossa Senhora da Cadeira
notes: [Aviceiro] A former small chapel at Cadeirinha, in Aviceiro.

own_entry.abstract: Former chapel at the sítio of Cadeirinha, within the present parish of Quinta Grande; the entry also mentions a hermitage to Our Lady called the chapel of Porta da Quinta in the same parish.

payload.name: Capela dos Santos Cosme e Damião
notes: [Lombo do Salão] Former chapel founded in 1681 at Lombo do Salão.

own_entry.abstract: Long-vanished chapel at Salão, Calheta, founded in 1681 by the surgeon António de França Gomes.

Opening part of the long entry on Madeira's levadas (irrigation channels), explaining their origin in the needs of the first settlers and their central importance to Madeiran agriculture and to feeding a dense, growing population.
Discusses the geographical terms for coastal inlets and reserves the name 'bay' in the archipelago for those of Funchal and Porto Santo, calling the rest 'enseadas'.
A locality beyond Ribeiro Frio on the road to Santana, known for fine views towards the Ribeira da Metade and Pico do Areeiro.
A Funchal street north of the Municipal Garden, named after the explorer Roberto Ivens by council decision in 1885.
A large natural opening in the rocks of Ponta do Furado at Ponta de São Lourenço, resembling a great doorway.
A scenic viewpoint near Monte Mendonho in the São Vicente mountains.

Describes the chapels dedicated to Saint Mary Magdalene in Madeira: the ruined Manueline chapel at Madalena in Santo António parish (Funchal), one at Florenças in Arco da Calheta, and an old chapel in Porto Moniz that serves as a curacy seat and pilgrimage centre.
A mountain peak in the parish of Ponta Delgada offering fine views.
An inhabited locality in Ponta Delgada parish, site of the Quinta da Palmeira, now the bishop's residence.

The Mosteiro Novo was an unfinished convent begun in Funchal by Canon Manuel Afonso Rocha in the 17th century, whose building later housed the Diocesan Seminary for most of the period from 1697 to 1909 and again after 1911.

payload.name: Capelas de Nossa Senhora da Consolação

own_entry.abstract: Describes four Madeiran chapels dedicated to Our Lady of Consolation: at the Ornelas entailed estate in Caniço, in Santa Luzia (Funchal), at Foro in Estreito de Câmara de Lobos, and a former one in Arco da Calheta.
History of Funchal's slaughterhouses and meat markets from the fifteenth century to the modern municipal slaughterhouse of 1941.

Rua Direita is an old street in the Sé parish of Funchal. It was once one of the city's largest and most important streets, where the bishop D. Jerónimo Barreto lived and where the church and hostel of São Bartolomeu stood.
Funchal street, formerly Rua Nova de Santa Maria, linking Largo dos Lavradores with Largo das Torneiras, renamed in 1911.

Describes the small rock-cut chapel of the Almas Pobres in Funchal, between the convents of Santa Clara and Mercês, built in 1781 by Roque José de Araujo and tied to a local legend about the souls in purgatory. It also mentions an older chapel of the same name in Santa Maria Maior parish, founded around 1470.

payload.name: Cais em frente da entrada da Cidade

own_entry.headword: Cais em frente da entrada da Cidade
own_entry.abstract: History of the quay at the Entrada da Cidade in Funchal, from the failed municipal stone quay begun in 1843 to the state-built quay completed in 1892 and its extension inaugurated in 1933.

The 'Cortina da Cidade' was the circuit of walls that defended Funchal by land and sea, begun under D. Sebastião and completed in 1689. The entry traces its construction and financing, and its gradual demolition, with its gates, in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries.
Brief account of chapels dedicated to Saint Sebastian in Ponta do Sol, Porto Santo, Santa Cruz and São Jorge, with notes on their rebuilding in the eighteenth century.
A short history of the cemeteries of Funchal and Madeira, built from 1836 onwards to replace burial inside churches.
Two small islets, do Guincho and das Ceroulas, off the coast of Seixal, also called the Seixal islets.

A square in Funchal on the left bank of the João Gomes stream, formerly the site of a Saturday fair selling poles and stakes for vine trellises, and home to the main entrance of the Mercado dos Lavradores, opened in 1939.
A sítio (locality) in the parish of Faial.
A small beach in Funchal, east of the Santiago fortress and below the parish church of Santa Maria Maior, made easily accessible as a bathing beach by Funchal council in 1939.
A small spring near the foot of Pico Ruivo at about 1,870 metres, believed by the Elucidário to be the highest spring in Madeira, with clear, cold water but little flow in summer.

The Travessa is the popular name for the stretch of sea, about 27 miles long, between Madeira (Ilhéu de Fora off Ponta de São Lourenço) and Porto Santo (Ilhéu de Baixo or da Cal). It is known for storms and generally rough seas.

Entry on the chapels dedicated to St John the Baptist in Madeira, chiefly the fifteenth-century São João da Ribeira chapel in Funchal, early seat of the Franciscans, with shorter notes on chapels of the same dedication in Ponta do Sol, Câmara de Lobos, Calheta, Campanário and Santana.
Locality in Monte parish containing the parish church, where Emperor Charles of Austria is buried, and the chapel of Nossa Senhora da Conceição.
Locality in Quinta Grande parish where the chapel of Santo António, built in 1884 at the Quinta do Pombal, stands.

payload.name: Avenida de Pedro Jose de Ornelas

own_entry.abstract: Funchal avenue, formerly the Caminho da Pena, named after a president of the municipal council who died in 1878.
Funchal street, formerly Rua do Aljube, renamed in 1919 after naval officer Carvalho de Araújo, killed in 1918 defending the steamer San Miguel.
The 'Casa de Dona Mécia' is an old building in the Rua dos Aranhas, Funchal, formerly a teacher-training school and Protestant chapel, classified as a property of public interest in 1940.

payload.name: Convento de Nossa Senhora ds Piedade

own_entry.headword: Convento de Nossa Senhora ds Piedade
own_entry.abstract: Former Franciscan convent in Madeira founded by the Genoese settler Urbano Lomelino, who left his estate entailed to finish and maintain it; after the religious orders were abolished it returned to his heirs, and no trace of it now survives.
A chapel dedicated to Our Lady of Fátima at Pico do Galo, Câmara de Lobos, founded by Father António de Abreu Vieira and blessed in 1931.

payload.name: Capelas de Nossa Senhora da Fé

own_entry.abstract: Two chapels dedicated to Our Lady of Faith, one founded in São Martinho in 1668 and another at Porto da Cruz in the 1820s, the latter now vanished.

payload.name: Capela de Nossa Senhora da Glória

own_entry.abstract: A chapel of Our Lady of Glory in Campanário, founded in 1599 and restored by the Countess of Torre Bela.

payload.name: Capela de Nossa Senhora de Jesus

own_entry.abstract: The earliest known chapel of Our Lady of Jesus, founded in São Martinho in 1656 by João Bettencourt de Atouguia.

payload.name: Capelas de Nossa Senhora do Livramento

own_entry.abstract: Chapels of Our Lady of Deliverance in Caniço, Ponta do Sol, Monte, Estreito da Calheta and São Vicente, with founders and dates; the Caniço one was a pilgrimage site.
Describes three former chapels dedicated to Santa Quitéria in Madeira: at Pico do Cardo in Santo António parish (1727), at Lombo da Estrela in Calheta (1724), and at Madalena do Mar.
Monte Gordo or Piedade, a seaward height in Caniçal parish crowned by the chapel of Nossa Senhora da Piedade, a landmark for ships, said to have been founded in the 16th century by Garcia Moniz.
Inhabited locality in Jardim do Mar parish with the chapel of Nossa Senhora da Piedade and manor of the Couto Cardoso entail, founded 1730 and rebuilt 1825.
Funchal street linking Rua da Carreira with Rua das Cruzes, named in 1895 in honour of the poet Manuel Caetano Pimenta de Aguiar.
Small locality, also called Quinta dos Ferreiros, in the parish of Calheta, where a chapel of Nossa Senhora da Penha was built in 1682.
A chapel of Our Lady Mother of Men on the Caminho do Meio, Santa Maria Maior, owned by the Visconde de Cacongo.

payload.name: Capelas de Nossa Senhora dos Milagres

own_entry.abstract: Two chapels of Our Lady of Miracles, in Monte (1661) and Ponta do Sol (1662).

payload.name: Capela de Nossa Senhora do Monserrate

own_entry.abstract: A long-vanished chapel of Our Lady of Montserrat near the old pillory of Calheta.

History of the town and municipality of Santa Cruz in eastern Madeira, raised to a vila in 1515 within the captaincy of Machico, with its customs house, Misericórdia, rivalry with Machico and later boundary changes.

Entry on the parish of Santana on Madeira's north coast, praised as the most picturesque of the north. It covers its settlement, its creation from São Jorge in the 16th century, its parish priests, its church, its localities and its population.

Cabo Girão is a sheer sea cliff on Madeira's south coast, some 600 metres high and among the tallest in the world, named according to Frutuoso as the end of the first day's circuit of the discovery voyage. The entry covers the name, the viewpoint built around 1935 and a public works director's account of its height.
Stream rising at Picos da Silva and da Relva, dividing Estreito da Calheta and Prazeres parishes.
A stream of the same name crossing São Jorge parish.
A shoal off the coast of Achadas da Cruz.
Coastal projection bounding the Abra inlet to the east, near Ponta de São Lourenço.
A small islet off the northern shore of the Ponta de São Lourenço, at the eastern end of Madeira.
Ponta Branca, also called Ponta de Nordeste, is a headland on the north-east coast of Porto Santo.
A small channel separating the tip of Ponta de São Lourenço from the Ilhéu de Agostinho, fordable at low tide.
A square in Funchal beside the Campo do Almirante Reis, notable for its ornamental fountain.
Former name of the Funchal street now called Rua dos Tanoeiros, explained by a quotation from Frutuoso about a well at its end.
Man-made pits in Madeira's mountains that stored winter hail and snow to supply ice for sorbets in summer, now abandoned.

payload.name: Capelas de Nossa Senhora da Conceição

own_entry.abstract: Survey of the chapels in Madeira dedicated to Our Lady of the Conception, with their founders and dates, from the 16th century to 1930, including the Capela-Monumento at Babosas (Monte) built in 1906 to mark the jubilee of the Immaculate Conception dogma.

payload.name: Lombada, Ribeira e Capela de São Pedro

own_entry.headword: São Pedro (Lombada, Ribeira e Capela de)
own_entry.abstract: Describes the Lombada de São Pedro in Santa Cruz parish, the stream crossing it (also called Ribeira da Boaventura), and the chapel of São Pedro founded there in the early 16th century, destroyed by the 1803 flood and rebuilt.

payload.name: Capela de São Pedro Gonçalves Telmo

own_entry.abstract: Notes a former chapel of São Pedro Gonçalves Telmo near the beach at Calheta, referring to the entry Corpo Santo.
A small point on the north-west coast of Porto Santo at Fonte da Areia.
A locality on Porto Santo's north coast with a drinking fountain, a popular excursion spot.
A 1,560 m peak on the Paul da Serra plateau.
A pleasant spot with a clear spring at Fanal in the uplands of Ribeira da Janela.
A roadside spot with a drinking fountain built in 1847 on the road from Santo António to Curral das Freiras.

Entry on the parish of Tábua, in the municipality of Ribeira Brava, covering the origin of its name, its creation and clergy stipends, its parish church and chapels, early settlers and principal localities.

payload.name: Capelas de Nossa Senhora da Vida

own_entry.abstract: Two chapels dedicated to Nossa Senhora da Vida: one founded by Manuel Valente in 1679 in São Pedro parish, location unknown, and another founded by Inês Teixeira at Fajã do Mar.

payload.name: Capela de Nossa Senhora das Vitórias

own_entry.abstract: A former chapel of Nossa Senhora das Vitórias in Machico, built in 1749.

payload.name: Capela de Nosso Senhor Jesus Cristo

own_entry.abstract: Fifteenth-century chapel founded by Gil Anes in Santa Cruz, later the seat of an entailed estate.
Funchal street opened after the 1803 flood, parallel to Rua de Santa Maria, now named Latino Coelho.

payload.name: Nova Aldeia ou Aldeia da Rainha

own_entry.headword: Nova Aldeia ou Aldeia da Rainha
own_entry.abstract: Short-lived settlement founded by royal charter in 1768 in Santo da Serra for families moved from Porto Santo.
A small stream rising on the Pico da Fonte do Barro.
A small stream rising on the Pico da Pedreira.
One of the longest and fullest streams of Madeira, rising in the Paul da Serra, Rabaçal springs and Assobiadouro.
The São Vicente stream, rising on the Ferreiros and Cumeada peaks and fed by the Ribeira Grande and Atalho brook.
A stream rising in the Serra da Boaventura, shorter than the Ribeira do Porco.
One of the fullest streams of Madeira, rising at Boca das Torrinhas and called Ribeira do Porco near the village.
The São Jorge stream, rising on the Pico do Canário and fed by the Canário, Grande and Tombo da Furna brooks.
A stream rising on Pico Ruivo, also called Ribeira Seca, fed by the Ribeira da Metade and Ribeiro Frio.
A Funchal alley linking the Travessa do Rego and Travessa da Conveniência; in 1902 the council allowed part of it to be closed off.
Former Funchal street, later Rua das Hortas and now Rua do Alferes Veiga Pestana, named after the Vale brook.

Entry on the parish of Nossa Senhora do Monte (commonly 'Monte') above Funchal, covering its origin in Adão Gonçalves Ferreira's chapel, the legend of the Virgin's apparition, the building of the church, the island-wide cult and August pilgrimage, and its quintas, railway and toboggans.

payload.name: Porto e Cais da Ribeira Brava

own_entry.abstract: Describes the landing place of Ribeira Brava, a pebble beach where embarking was difficult, and the quay built there between 1904 and 1908, linked to the town by a tunnel and a short road and served by coastal steamers.

payload.name: Capelas de Nossa Senhora do Amparo

own_entry.abstract: Describes several chapels in Madeira dedicated to Our Lady of Amparo, chiefly the one at Álamos (Água de Mel) in Santo António, seat of the Água de Mel entail, with others in São Martinho, Ponta do Pargo and Machico.

payload.name: Capelas de Nossa Senhora da Boa Viagem

own_entry.headword: Nossa Senhora da Boa Viagem (Capelas de)
own_entry.abstract: Describes two chapels dedicated to Our Lady of Good Voyage: one founded in 1711 at Carne Azeda in Santa Luzia, and an ancient one in Santa Maria Maior, Funchal, founded by Bento da Veiga, whose adjoining house reputedly held the first customs house.

payload.name: Capela de Nossa Senhora do Bom Despacho

own_entry.headword: Nossa Senhora do Bom Despacho (Capela de)
own_entry.abstract: A chapel in Campanário founded in 1672 by the morgado Jerónimo de Atouguia Bettencourt and his wife, rebuilt in 1762, and still owned by the Brito family in 1921.

payload.name: Capelas de Nossa Senhora do Bom Sucesso

own_entry.headword: Nossa Senhora do Bom Sucesso (Capelas de)
own_entry.abstract: Describes three chapels of Our Lady of Good Success: one at Garachico straddling the boundary of Câmara de Lobos and Estreito de Câmara de Lobos, one at Lombo da Estrela in Calheta (1683), and one on the Caminho do Meio in Funchal owned by the municipal council.
A square in Funchal by the Rua da Carreira, where the bishop's palace has its main entrance, on the site of the old British cemetery demolished in 1888.

Entry on the parish of São Jorge on Madeira's north coast, covering its early settlement and grants of land, the creation of the parish in the mid-sixteenth century, and its eighteenth-century church with notable gilded woodwork and sculpture. It also lists the parish's main localities and its population in 1921.
Describes the Stations of the Passion oratories that stood in Funchal streets and at which the Procession of the Passos halted.
Describes the first, unsuccessful attempt by the Funchal Municipal Council, before constitutional government, to found a charitable home for orphans and invalids.

payload.name: Cais na Ilha do Porto Santo

own_entry.headword: Cais na Ilha do Porto Santo
own_entry.abstract: Notes the pier serving Porto Santo and an abandoned 1824 plan for a mole and quay at the Baixas de São Tiago in Funchal.
A 628 m peak on the northern coast of Caniçal parish.
A hill in Machico parish with wide views, on whose slopes rebel and government troops clashed on 2 May 1931.
Mountain pass separating the Boaventura serra from that of Curral das Freiras, noted for Sedum farinosum and Isoplexis sceptrum.
A site at about 750 m between Pico do Arco and Pico do Canário, starting point of a path to Ribeira da Boaventura.
A viewpoint east of Pico do Areeiro with a fine panorama on clear days.
A site near Pico Grande at about 1300 m overlooking Curral das Freiras and Serra de Água valley.
A peak at about 1135 m in Estreito de Câmara de Lobos parish, near Boca dos Namorados.
A 1300 m elevation of the same name in the serra of Ribeira da Janela.

Entry on the town and municipality of Machico, describing its valley setting and tracing its municipal history, from its probable creation around 1451 through territorial losses to Santa Cruz, São Vicente and Santana, to its arms, privileges and new town hall of 1929.

Entry on Santo António, the most populous suburban parish of Funchal, covering its origins as a curacy c.1557, clergy stipends, the building of its parish churches, chapels, sítios and later improvements.
Memorial in the Angústias cemetery to those killed by German submarine shells at Funchal on 3 December 1916, handed to the municipal council in 1917.
Notes that Madeiran churches have few notable tombs, citing the Brandão family mausoleums in the Carmo church and the tomb in Santa Clara said to hold Zargo.

Explains the particular Madeiran meaning of 'quinta', a walled country or suburban estate with a fine house, gardens and often farmland and a chapel, and lists the island's most notable quintas and their owners.

Suburban parish of Funchal, separated from São Pedro and created under a royal charter of 1579, named after its original chapel of São Roque. The entry traces the history of its parish church and lists its chapels, principal localities and population.

Reproduces the 1896 chemical and bacteriological analysis by Charles Lepierre of the cold spring water of São Roque at Machico, long reputed for its therapeutic virtues. The water was classed as hypothermal, hyposaline and sodium-chloride, and found free of coliform bacteria.
The mortuary at the Angústias cemetery in Funchal, built by order of the municipal council in 1900 to hold bodies of the poor and unclaimed.
Former lane in Santa Maria parish, Funchal, named after Canon Vicente Nery da Silva, later widened and renamed Caminho do Acciaioly.
A reef or shoal lying east of the harbour of São Vicente, not far from the coast.

payload.name: Capela de São João e Santana

own_entry.abstract: A chapel built in 1814 at the Quinta do Trapiche in Santo António by João António de Gouveia Rego; its adjoining house later housed the seminary.

payload.name: Capela de Nossa Senhora do Pilar

own_entry.abstract: A private chapel and quinta at the Pilar site in São Martinho parish, Funchal, founded in 1676 by Gonçalo de Freitas Drumond.

payload.name: Capelas de Nossa Senhora dos Prazeres

own_entry.abstract: Two chapels dedicated to Nossa Senhora dos Prazeres: one founded in 1611 by Tristão Gomes de Castro in Monte (later Santa Luzia), and an entailed one in Santa Maria Maior.

payload.name: Capelas de Nossa Senhora das Preces

own_entry.abstract: Three chapels of Nossa Senhora das Preces, in Santo António (c.1708), Câmara de Lobos (1683) and Machico, each giving its name to the surrounding site.

payload.name: Capela de Nossa Senhora dos Remédios e Amparo

own_entry.headword: Nossa Senhora dos Remédios e Amparo (Capela de)
own_entry.abstract: A chapel attached to the manor house of the viscounts of São João on Rua das Maravilhas, built by Dr. Rui Bettencourt da Câmara and blessed on 1 January 1940.

Parish at the western tip of Madeira's south coast, in the municipality of Calheta, named after a huge pargo fish caught there during the discovery voyage. The entry covers its creation from Fajã da Ovelha, its church, schools, entailed estates, farming, levadas, lighthouse and administrative history.
A small plateau in the Serra do Poiso, close to its shelter house.

History of the Convent of Nossa Senhora da Incarnação in Funchal, founded in 1650 by Canon Henrique Calaça de Viveiros to celebrate Portugal's restoration of independence, and of the later uses of its site as a British barracks, the diocesan seminary and offices of the Junta Geral.
A mountain peak in the uplands of the parish of Fajã da Ovelha, not far from the Pico da Fonte do Bispo.
A headland on the coast of the parish of Fajã da Ovelha.
A locality in the uplands of Faial parish with a small shelter house for travellers.
An inhabited locality in Arco da Calheta with the chapel of Nossa Senhora da Vida, founded in 1663 by Inez Teixeira.
Inhabited locality in the parish of Caniço, named after a former chapel of Nossa Senhora do Livramento whose popular pilgrimage has moved to the parish church.
Inhabited locality in the parish of Monte, named after its entailed chapel of Nossa Senhora do Livramento (1684); it also has a recent chapel of the Sacred Heart.
Locality in Ponta do Sol parish with a chapel of Nossa Senhora do Livramento built in 1656 as seat of an entail.
Locality in São Vicente parish named after its chapel of Nossa Senhora do Livramento, founded in 1683.
Entry on the municipality of Ribeira Brava, created in 1914 from parishes of Ponta do Sol and Câmara de Lobos, and on its seat, the sítio of Lugar, raised to the status of vila in 1928.

payload.name: Populaçâo, Superficie e Situaçâo Geográfica da ilha do Porto Santo

own_entry.headword: Porto Santo (Populaçâo, Superficie e Situaçâo Geográfica da ilha do)
own_entry.abstract: Statistical entry on the island of Porto Santo, giving its population from 1529 to 1940, the differing estimates of its surface area, and its geographical coordinates.

History of the João Diniz springs beside the São Lourenço fortress in Funchal, a long-used public water source for townspeople and ships, which disappeared in November 1939 during repairs to the palace.

Survey of the oldest surviving civil and religious buildings of Madeira, especially Funchal houses with Gothic twin-light windows, most since demolished, and the churches noted as late Gothic by Dr Neale in 1844.

History of the quarantine station (lazaretto) of Funchal, from unrealised plans in 1816 through temporary sites to the buildings at the mouth of the Ribeira de Gonçalo Aires (1866–74), later used for epidemics and political prisoners.

payload.name: Capelas de Nossa Senhora da Nazaré

own_entry.abstract: Describes three Madeiran chapels dedicated to Nossa Senhora da Nazaré, in Arco da Calheta, Câmara de Lobos and São Martinho. It gives their founders and dates, and a fishermen's tradition about the lady of the entail at Câmara de Lobos.
List of the principal headlands (pontas) of Madeira, Porto Santo and the Desertas, grouped by municipality.
The former fortification on the Pico do Castelo in Porto Santo, built under Philippine rule after the Moorish raid of 1617 as a refuge from pirates rather than a true stronghold.
A viewpoint hill in Santo António parish overlooking Funchal, where a commemorative cross was inaugurated in 1941.

A reconstruction of the layout of Funchal in 1508, when the town was raised to city status, describing which streets, churches, chapels, convents and other buildings already existed and which came later.
Describes the mountain refuge huts built in the high serras of Madeira to shelter travellers caught by storms, listing those existing at the time and noting their poor state and staffing.

History of provision for the mentally ill in Madeira, from a 1493 request for a 'Tronco' to the founding of the Manicómio Câmara Pestana at the Quinta do Rochedo (1906) and the Casa de Saúde de São João de Deus at the Trapiche (1922–24).

payload.name: Aspectos Hidrográficos: Baias, Enseadas, Portos e Praias da Madeira

own_entry.headword: Madeira (Aspectos Hidrográficos: Baias, Enseadas, Portos e Praias da)
own_entry.abstract: Survey of Madeira's coastline features: the two bays (Funchal and Porto Santo), the small coves, the landing places graded as good, fair or poor, and the island's mostly pebble beaches. It serves as an index pointing to the individual entries on each port and beach.

own_entry.headword: Ponta do Sol (Vila e Município da)
own_entry.abstract: History of the town and municipality of Ponta do Sol, an early sugar-producing centre raised to a town in 1501, tracing the changes in its municipal territory and its role as seat of a judicial district (comarca).
A locality in São Martinho with the chapel of Nossa Senhora do Amparo, founded in 1712 by D. Luísa de Mendonça and belonging to the Sauvaire entail.
A locality in Ponta do Pargo named after its chapel of Nossa Senhora do Amparo, whose feast draws people from neighbouring parishes.
Lists the main headlands of the Desertas group: Ponta de Santa Maria, Castanheira, Pedregal and Ponta das Agulhas.
Survey of the coastal and water features of Porto Santo: its great southern bay and beach, minor landing places, shoals, islets, the raised fossil beach and the island's small seasonal streams.
Águas Doces is the name of a small beach and stretch of coast near Funchal, lying between the Ilhéu da Pontinha and the mouth of the Ribeiro Seco.
Describes Madeira's iron-bearing springs, chiefly the Jamboto spring in Santo António, analysed by Carlos Lepierre in 1900.
Survey of chapels dedicated to Saint Joseph in Madeira and Porto Santo, with their founders and dates, in Ribeira Brava, Calheta, Porto Santo, Machico, Santa Cruz and Camacha.
The Praça do Município in Funchal, formerly the Largo do Colégio, created in 1836 on part of the churchyard of São João Evangelista and greatly enlarged in 1943–44.
The lighthouse on the Ilhéu de Cima off Porto Santo, which began operating in 1901, forty years after the São Lourenço light, after coastal shipwrecks had shown the need for it.
The lighthouse at Ponta do Pargo, western end of Madeira's south coast, built before the First World War but only inaugurated on 5 June 1922.

Survey of the history of Madeira's coastal fortifications, from the first requests for a fortress at Funchal in the fifteenth century to anti-submarine batteries built in 1916–17. It lists the forts, redoubts and batteries built in each period across Madeira and Porto Santo.
A cave or sea grotto on the western coast of Deserta Grande in the Desertas Islands.
A coastal point in Câmara de Lobos parish near Cabo Girão, midway between Fajã das Pedras and Fajã dos Asnos.

History of the prison (cadeia) of the Funchal judicial district, from its old house on the Rua da Cadeia Velha, through nearly a century in the building on the Largo da Sé, to the new prison built on the site of the São Lázaro hospital in 1913.

payload.name: Capela de Nossa Senhora de Belém

own_entry.abstract: Extinct chapel of Our Lady of Bethlehem at Câmara de Lobos, founded in 1649 and rebuilt in 1758; also notes a namesake chapel at Porto da Cruz.

payload.name: Capelas de Nossa Senhora da Boa Hora

own_entry.headword: Nossa Senhora da Boa Hora (Capelas de)
own_entry.abstract: Chapels of Our Lady of Boa Hora at Torre (Câmara de Lobos), above Funchal (1726) and at Fajã in Arco da Calheta.

payload.name: Capela de Nossa Senhora da Boa Nova

own_entry.headword: Nossa Senhora da Boa Nova (Capela de)
own_entry.abstract: Chapel of Our Lady of Boa Nova in São Gonçalo parish, founded in 1701.
The municipality of Santana on Madeira's north coast, created in 1835, briefly abolished in 1867 and losing Porto da Cruz to Machico in 1852.
A small ruined chapel of Santa Apolónia that belonged to the former Franciscan convent in Calheta.
A lost chapel of Santa Brígida in São Pedro parish, Funchal, founded in 1668; its site is unknown.

Parish on the north coast of Madeira, in the municipality of São Vicente, separated from Ponta Delgada in 1836; the entry covers its obscure name, church history, levadas, localities and a local anecdote about General Beresford.

Describes the chapels dedicated to Saint Paul in Madeira, chiefly the ancient chapel on the Largo de São Paulo in Funchal founded by João Gonçalves Zarco, which briefly housed the parish of São Pedro, and a ruined chapel at Porto Moniz.
A small, poor landing place on the coast of Campanário parish, where a modest landing stage was built in 1909.
Funchal square built 1898–1901 to improve Santa Maria Maior, named after King Carlos and renamed Campo do Almirante Reis in 1911.

Describes two chapels dedicated to São Luís: an early eighteenth-century chapel at Diferença in Faial, and the chapel built by Bishop D. Luís Figueiredo de Lemos beside the old Episcopal Palace in Funchal, where he was buried.
A locality in the parish of Machico, within the inhabited sítio of Marco, named after the chapel of Nossa Senhora das Preces, founded in 1750.
An inhabited locality in the parish of Santo António, Funchal, with a chapel of Nossa Senhora das Preces built in 1768.
Caminho Grande or Preces, a sítio in the parish of Câmara de Lobos, with the chapels of Nossa Senhora das Preces (1683) and Nossa Senhora da Nazaré (1757) and the ruins of a São Cândido chapel.

Explains that 'Norte da Ilha' is the common name for Madeira's northern coast, from Ponta do Tristão to Ponta de São Lourenço, covering the municipalities of Porto Moniz, São Vicente and Santana and the parish of Porto da Cruz.
A small maritime disinfection station operating at the Pontinha in Funchal since 1901, funded through the Junta Geral and staffed by government-paid personnel.
The municipal medical post of Funchal, opened in 1889 by the town council, which acquired an X-ray apparatus in 1922.
Small quay at Ponta da Oliveira in Caniço, built in 1909 and linked to the main road by a 1,800-metre branch.

payload.name: Porto e Praia do Arco de São Jorge

own_entry.headword: Arco de São Jorge (Porto e Praia do)
own_entry.abstract: A small, poor landing place with a short beach on the coast of the parish of Arco de São Jorge, where disembarking is difficult.
Introduction to Madeira's twenty-six quays, mostly built or improved by the Junta Geral between 1905 and 1916, which eased coastal landings and inter-parish communication.

Reproduces a 1924 newspaper article on the restoration of the old organ of the extinct Convent of Santa Clara in Funchal, said to have been given by João Gonçalves Zarco's children in 1498. It also mentions the similar restoration of the Machico parish church organ.

Discusses the successive residences of João Gonçalves Zargo in Funchal: a wooden house by the Santa Catarina chapel, a stone house near São Paulo, and his final home near the Conceição de Cima (Santa Clara) church, identified by the author with the present Quinta das Cruzes. It also traces the later owners of that house and the two-handed sword attributed to Zargo.
A locality in the parish of Estreito da Calheta with a chapel of Nossa Senhora da Conceição built in 1673, once the seat of one of Madeira's largest entailed estates.
A locality in Ribeira Brava named after its chapel of the Conceição, whose founder and date are unknown.
An inhabited locality in São Roque, Funchal, with a chapel of Nossa Senhora da Conceição built in 1700.
A shoal near the Ilhéu da Lapa off the coast of Campanário.
A square in Funchal, commonly called Largo das Babosas, named after the Capela-Monumento of the Conceição built in 1906 to mark the dogma's fiftieth anniversary.

Pico Ruivo is the highest peak of Madeira, lying at the southern edge of Santana parish; the entry describes the routes to its summit, the historical measurements of its height (1,861 m according to the 1914 geodetic survey), its panorama, vegetation and geology, and the shelter built there in 1939.

payload.name: Porto e Ribeira de São Vicente

own_entry.abstract: Describes the small, difficult landing place at São Vicente on Madeira's north coast and the São Vicente stream, with its chapel on a basalt rock at the mouth and a nearby lava cave.
Notes on three chapels dedicated to St Francis, in Calheta, São Pedro (São Francisco das Furnas) and Santa Luzia.

payload.name: Capela de Sao Francisco de Borja

own_entry.abstract: Chapel of St Francis Borgia built in 1760 by D. Francisco de Vasconcelos at Cruz da Guarda, Porto da Cruz, correcting the 'Saudades' attribution to St Francis Xavier.
Chapels of St Francis Xavier in Calheta (1693), Santa Cruz (1684) and Porto da Cruz.
History of the Funchal street beside the Jardim Municipal, opened in 1814 through the former Franciscan convent grounds and renamed in 1885 after the explorer Hermenegildo Capelo.
Former name of a stretch of the present Rua Correia Heredia in Funchal, between Rua da Figueira Preta and Rua do Bom Jesus.
Funchal street, formerly Rua dos Aranhas, named after Dr Chaves, a graduate of the Funchal medical-surgical school and member of the town council.

payload.name: Enseada e Porto do Lugar de Baixo

own_entry.headword: Lugar de Baixo (Enseada e Porto do)
own_entry.abstract: A small cove and beach landing at Lugar de Baixo, sometimes better for landing than the quays of Ponta do Sol and Ribeira Brava; Infante D. Luís landed there in 1858.

payload.name: Capela de Nossa Senhora do Carmo

own_entry.abstract: Chapel of Our Lady of Mount Carmel built in 1658 by the merchant Domingos Rodrigues on his estate in Campanário.

payload.name: Igreja de Nossa Senhora do Carmo

own_entry.abstract: Carmo church in Funchal, built 1656–1660 for the Third Order of Carmel, which gave its name to its street and holds the island's only artistically notable mausoleums.

Rua dos Ferreiros is one of Funchal's busiest streets, running from Rua 5 de Outubro to the Torreão bridge; the entry explains its former names (Peru, Estudo, Pinheiro) and their origins. It was renamed Rua do Comércio in 1915.
Pico de Baixo is a hill in the northern part of Porto Santo island, towards the east-south-east.

Survey of the Madeira archipelago: its historical and scientific importance, geographical position, extreme points, coordinates, area and population, and its status as the administrative district of Funchal.
A small landing place with a short beach on the coast of Gaula parish.

Describes the earliest dwellings built in Madeira after its discovery, which were made of timber from the native forests, and records traditions about the first two-storey house and the first stone houses in Funchal.

A survey of the chapels dedicated to Saint Anthony across Madeira, giving for each its parish, founder, date of construction or blessing and later fate. It covers surviving, rebuilt and vanished chapels from the 16th to the early 20th century.

own_entry.headword: Madeira (Aspectos orográficos: Encostas, Planaltos e Vales)
own_entry.abstract: A survey of Madeira's relief: the central east–west mountain range and its peaks, the few plateaux, the main coastal headlands and the principal valleys. It explains the traditional division of the island into a North Coast and a South Coast.
Brief account of early attempts to light the coasts of Madeira, notably an unsuccessful 1861 parliamentary bill for lighthouses at Ponta de São Lourenço and the Pontinha islet.
Short entry on the small fixed-light beacon on the islet at Funchal harbour, known as 'a brasa do ilhéu', in service from 1866 until replaced in 1931.

Part 1 of the entry on Funchal Cathedral, a Gothic-Manueline national monument begun in the 1490s under D. Manuel and consecrated in 1516, covering its construction history, architecture, Mudéjar cedar ceiling, chapels, processional cross and organs, followed by the start of a chronology.

Describes the harbour of Porto do Moniz, reputedly the safest and most sheltered anchorage on Madeira's north coast, used as a refuge when southerly winds close the southern ports. It records hydrographic studies of 1914 and harbour works carried out between 1901 and 1916.
A locality in the parish of Serra de Água where Funchal Municipal Council owned a small property, sold in 1918.

Entry on the parish of Machico, landing place of the discoverers Zargo and Tristão Vaz and seat of the captaincy of Machico, covering its discovery, the founding of the parish c. 1450, its clergy and stipends, chapels, historical events, mineral springs, localities, population and notable natives.

payload.name: Baixa, Enseada e Porto dos Barbeiros

own_entry.abstract: On Porto Santo, between the Ponta da Cruz and Ponta do Ninho do Guincho, lie the Barbeiros shoal, the Enseada dos Barbeiros (or de Guilherme) and a small landing place of the same name.

Entry on the parish of Ponta Delgada on Madeira's north coast, covering the origin of its name, the church of Senhor Bom Jesus and its ancient pilgrimage, its clergy, notable residents, agriculture and services.
The Ribeira da Janela, the longest and fullest stream in Madeira, rising on the Paul da Serra and feeding the Rabaçal levadas.

History of the municipality of Porto Moniz in north-western Madeira, created in 1835 after long local petitions, and repeatedly abolished and restored in the nineteenth century. Porto Moniz was never raised to the status of a vila, only serving as the seat of the concelho.

A small former building at the Entrada da Cidade in Funchal, used by the health guards who inspected arriving ships, later as town hall and as seat of the Port Captaincy and Commercial Association; sold by the council in 1914.
An 18th-century town house in Funchal at the corner of Rua da Conceição and Rua da Figueira Preta, named after the consulates once housed there and admired for its architecture.

First part of the entry on Funchal, covering the origin of its name (from the fennel plant, funcho), the creation of the town and municipality around 1451–52, and its elevation to city status by King Manuel I in 1508, with the royal charter transcribed in full.

Account of the public clocks of Madeira, above all the clock of Funchal Cathedral: the old clock made in 1775 and its replacement given by Dr Michael Grabham, installed in 1921–22. It also lists the other public clocks on the islands and the earlier custom of a paid official striking the hours.

This first part recounts the Hohenlohe concession of 1903 to build tuberculosis sanatoria in Madeira, the diplomatic dispute that led to its buyback by the Portuguese State in 1909, and reproduces Dr António de Lencastre's 1903 report and a 1914 government notice leasing the confiscated properties at Monte.

Entry on the parish of Câmara de Lobos, west of Funchal, covering the origin of its name in the discovery voyage of Zarco, its churches, chapels and collegiate chapter, early settlers, fishing community and renowned vineyards. It also records its localities, boundaries, levadas and population.
Peak of about 1,600 m among the heights surrounding Serra de Água parish.
Mountain in Madeira's central range, not far from Pico Ruivo.
Stream that is a tributary of the Ribeira de Machico.

General entry on Madeira's streams (ribeiras), which rise on the central mountain range and run through deep narrow valleys to the sea, torrential in winter and often dry in summer. It describes their destructive floods and introduces a list of the island's principal streams.
General entry on fajãs, the flats of land formed by landslides in Madeira. It lists the best-known examples and records notable landslips of 1689, 1804, 1856 and 1894.
The cold store planned by the Junta Agrícola in Funchal, built at considerable cost but never put into operation and abandoned in 1918.
Explains how the mountain range running east to west across Madeira divides the island into the north coast (Costa do Norte) and the south coast (Costa do Sul), with a rugged interior between them.

payload.name: Mercado e Capela de São Sebastião

own_entry.headword: Mercado e Capela de São Sebastião
own_entry.abstract: History of the ancient chapel of São Sebastião in Funchal, demolished in 1803 by Governor D. José Manuel da Câmara to build a market, rebuilt by the people in 1821 and demolished again by 1827, and of the square (now Largo do Comércio) with its marble fountain.

Lists chapels dedicated to Our Lady of Sorrows: the cemetery chapels of Santa Cruz, Câmara de Lobos and Angústias (Funchal), and the chapel of the Hospício da Princesa Dona Maria Amélia, whose image was given by Maximilian, later Emperor of Mexico.
Brief notes on three small quays: that of the Ilhéu de Fora (1870, for lighthouse staff), the Abra quay (1905) and the Caniçal landing stage (1909).
The Ponta da Oliveira landing stage (1909) and the Lazareto quay (probably 1866–74).
A private quay at Salto do Cavalo built by the industrialist Pedro da Cunha Pires.
The Palace Hotel quay on the Estrada Monumental, and the Wilson Company quay near Quinta do Calaça (c. 1903).
The Ponta da Cruz quay, with an older part and a modern part built around 1910 by the local cannery owners.
The Câmara de Lobos quay, begun by the government in 1876 and enlarged by the Junta Geral in 1903.
The small Campanário landing stage built by the Junta Geral in 1908.
The Pesqueiro landing stage built by the Junta Geral in 1916.
The Porto Moniz quay built by the Junta Geral in 1916, replacing a natural landing and a passenger ladder.
The Seixal quay, built by the Junta Geral between 1903 and 1916.
The São Jorge quay (1904–10) and the Pedra da Pescaria quay at Faial (1903–05), both by the Junta Geral.
The Porto da Cruz quay (1903) and the Ilhéu de Cima quay in Porto Santo (c. 1902) for lighthouse staff.

Entry on the parish of Porto do Moniz on Madeira's north-west coast, one of the oldest northern parishes, founded around the estate and chapel of Francisco Moniz, the Elder. It covers the origin of its name, its churches and chapels, the fort built against corsairs, and its localities and population.
Inhabited locality and small hill in Santo António parish, Funchal, famous as a viewpoint over the bay from Garajau to Cabo Girão. The name probably comes from the early settler Diogo Barcelos.
A high ridge above 1,700 metres near Pico Ruivo and the Homem em Pé basalt column, notable for rare plants.
The São Vicente ridge at 1,000 metres, from which both coasts are visible, reached by a road opened in 1916 and home to a very rare clubmoss.
A very old square in Funchal beside the Campo da Barca, demolished before 1860 and now part of the Praça de Tenerife.
A locality between Santana and Faial, noted for its fine views over Faial and the Penha de Águia and for its green, wooded road.

Entry on São Pedro, the most populous of Funchal's four urban parishes, where Zargo made the first settlement; it traces the parish's creation in 1566, suppression in 1579 and restoration in 1587, its clergy stipends, church building, chapels, notable institutions and boundaries.

General survey of the island of Madeira: its position, relief, streams, towns, scenery, roads, products, fauna, minerals, irrigation, trade and industries, and the origins, physical types and customs of its population. It serves as the umbrella article introducing the more detailed 'Madeira' sub-entries.

payload.name: Posto de Desinfecção do Campo da Barca

own_entry.headword: Posto de Desinfecção do Campo da Barca
own_entry.abstract: The public disinfection station at Campo da Barca in Funchal, built in 1904 and opened in 1905 by the Junta Geral, disinfected homes and public buildings after contagious diseases, notably during epidemics.

payload.name: Capela de Nossa Senhora da Paz

own_entry.abstract: Short entry on the chapel of Nossa Senhora da Paz, founded in 1621 by the priest Jerónimo da Silva in the parish of Santa Maria Maior, Funchal.

payload.name: Enseada, Porto e Cais de Machico

own_entry.abstract: Describes the bay, harbour and landing quays of Machico, one of the widest and most picturesque bays of the Madeira archipelago, with the history of its successive quays (1870–1873, 1905, 1907) and harbour lights (1931).
A small landing place on the south-south-west of Porto Santo.
Entry on Madeira's few upland plateaux, quoting a Portuguese dictionary that names four: Santo da Serra, Achada de Santa Ana, Paul da Serra and Achadas da Cruz.
A former charitable house in Funchal for poor and respectable widows, founded by João de Carvalhal in 1825 or 1826.
Introductory heading to brief notes on the few public monuments of Madeira.
An unfinished Funchal monument to the 1821 Constitution, demolished in 1823, whose foundations held a time capsule.
Bronze bust of bacteriologist Luís da Câmara Pestana erected in 1906 at the asylum garden in São Gonçalo, plus a 1913 plaque on his birthplace.

payload.name: Monumento comemorativo do Bombardeamento do Funchal

own_entry.headword: Monumento comemorativo do Bombardeamento do Funchal
own_entry.abstract: A small memorial to the bombardment of Funchal, in the old Angústias cemetery.
Monument in Funchal's Jardim Municipal commemorating the 1921 Lisbon–Funchal flight of Gago Coutinho and Sacadura Cabral.
Modest bust of João Fernandes Vieira inaugurated in 1924 on Avenida Arriaga and moved nine years later to the Jardim Municipal.

Entry on São Vicente, described as the largest and most populous parish of northern Madeira and seat of the only town on the north coast, covering its settlement, church history, localities, landscape and the deadly landslide of 1929.

payload.name: Capela de Nossa Senhora do Perpétuo Socorro

own_entry.headword: Nossa Senhora do Perpétuo Socorro (Capela de)
own_entry.abstract: A chapel dedicated to Nossa Senhora do Perpétuo Socorro, built at the sítio da Queimada in the parish of Água de Pena by Francisco de Freitas Correia. The printed year 1244 predates the settlement of Madeira and is presumably a misprint.
Describes Madeira's two capes, Cabo Garajau and Cabo Girão, their names, geology and botanical interest.

The Desertas are a group of three small uninhabited islands (Ilhéu Chão, Deserta Grande and Bugio) south-east of Madeira, near the Ponta de São Lourenço. The entry gives their position, distances, ecclesiastical attachment, history of ownership and sources.

Survey of the Madeira archipelago as a whole: its historical importance, composition, geographical position, extreme points, area, coastline, dimensions and population, with pointers to entries on the individual islands and the Funchal district.

payload.name: Ribeira e Porto de São Bartolomeu

own_entry.abstract: Stream rising on Paul da Serra dividing Calheta and Estreito da Calheta parishes, with a small landing place at its mouth.

payload.name: Forte de S. Felipe da Praça

own_entry.headword: Forte de S. Felipe da Praça
own_entry.abstract: A former fort in Funchal built in 1628 by the bishop-governor D. Jerónimo Fernando between the mouths of the João Gomes and Santa Luzia streams; it was later sold and replaced by a warehouse.

payload.name: Forte de Santo António da Alfândega

own_entry.headword: Forte de Santo António da Alfândega
own_entry.abstract: A redoubt built in 1644–45 on the walls of the Funchal Customs House to cover the beach with crossfire; it was later turned into warehouses.
The São Pedro or Forte Novo on the Calhau wall in Funchal, finished in 1707 under Duarte Sodré Pereira and notable for its furnace for heated shot; demolished in 1897.
An outwork built in 1712 to defend the Ribeiro Seco cove in Funchal, where British troops were quartered in 1801.
A 17th-century fort, traditionally built by a private individual, covering the Gonçalo Aires cove; Captain-General D. Diogo Coutinho wanted to put a silk factory there.
A fort built in 1708 on a rocky point east of Machico bay, which fired on a Miguelist brig in 1828 and became a cholera hospital in 1910.

payload.name: Forte de Nª Sª do Amparo

own_entry.headword: Forte de Nª Sª do Amparo
own_entry.abstract: A triangular fort at Machico built in 1706 without cost to the Crown, the last to surrender to the Miguelist landing of 1828.

payload.name: Forte de S. Roque de Machico

own_entry.headword: Forte de S. Roque de Machico
own_entry.abstract: A fort built during the Philippine period at the mouth of the Ribeirinho in Machico bay, of which only wall fragments remain.
A fort over the Caniçal cove built in the early 18th century after a pirate landing there.

payload.name: Forte de S. Bento da Ribeira Brava

own_entry.headword: Forte de S. Bento da Ribeira Brava
own_entry.abstract: A fort built by Governor Duarte Sodré Pereira to defend Ribeira Brava.
A list of the best-known waterfalls on Madeira island, grouped by the streams and valleys where they occur.
An inhabited locality in Água de Pena, Machico, with Madeira's first chapel to Our Lady of Perpetual Help (1924).
A Funchal street, formerly Rua do Oliveira and Rua Afonso Vaz, notorious in 1921 for its insanitary stables for hire horses and draught animals.
A peak on the boundary of Ribeira Brava and São Vicente, between Lombo do Mouro and Monte Medonho.

payload.name: Rua de Júlio da Silva Carvalho

own_entry.abstract: x

History of the town hall (Paços do Concelho) of Funchal: the eighteenth-century palace on Rua do Comércio bought by the municipal council in 1883, and the many buildings the council occupied from the fifteenth century onwards. It closes with brief notes on the town halls of the other Madeiran municipalities.

Describes the Quinta do Palheiro do Ferreiro, according to the Elucidário the finest and largest estate in Madeira, created by the 1st Count of Carvalhal in the early nineteenth century and later owned by John Blandy. It records royal visits and quotes an English visitor's description of 1826.
Lists several chapels in Madeira dedicated to the Souls in Purgatory, in Ribeira Brava, Estreito de Câmara de Lobos, Calheta and Ponta do Sol, several of them now lost or demolished.
Pico Branco is a mountain in the north-east of Porto Santo island, rising to 420 m above sea level.
Account of the Protestant churches of Funchal: the Anglican church in Rua da Bela Vista (completed 1822), a second Anglican church in Rua dos Aranhas (1848) and the Scottish church.
Former Funchal street between Largo do Colégio and Rua das Pretas, named after the chapel of Nossa Senhora da Piedade (the 'Igrejinha'), founded 1613 and demolished 1836.
Inhabited locality in Caniço parish, with ruins of a chapel of Nossa Senhora da Salvação founded in 1614.
Stream crossing Boaventura parish and reaching the sea near the Ribeira do Porco.
Stream in Ponta do Pargo parish.
Former name of part of Funchal's Rua das Mercês, named after a mill once there and originally called Rua do Peso.
Small islet off the coast of Porto Moniz parish.
Entry on the viewpoints (mirantes or miradouros) of Madeira, listing those in Funchal and elsewhere and recalling the viewpoints recommended by Civil Governor José Silvestre Ribeiro in 1850.

own_entry.headword: Manuel de Castro (Rampa e ponte de D.)
own_entry.abstract: A Funchal ramp and bridge named after governor D. Manuel de Portugal e Castro (1823–25), who built the bridge and widened the ramp.
Describes the 'Vapor', a curious red wooden building spanning the Santa Luzia stream in Funchal, built in 1837 as a café and bathhouse and demolished around 1898.

Lists the buildings and works of art in the Funchal district classified as national monuments or as properties of public interest under the decrees published in the Diário do Governo in 1940 and 1943.

payload.name: Ilha da Deserta Grande ou somente Deserta

own_entry.headword: Deserta Grande ou somente Deserta (Ilha da)
own_entry.abstract: The largest of the three Desertas islands, a steep, nearly flat-topped island with scant brackish water, never permanently inhabited but used for hunting, orchil gathering, grazing and some cereal growing. The entry covers its geography, history, fauna and notable episodes such as a 1503 corsair attack and an 1894 landslide.
The popular name for Madeira's south coast west of Funchal, covering the municipalities of Câmara de Lobos, Ribeira Brava, Ponta do Sol and Calheta.
The popular name for Madeira's south coast east of Funchal, covering the municipalities of Santa Cruz and Machico except the north-coast parish of Porto da Cruz.
Entry on Funchal's public markets, chiefly the Mercado de S. João, opened in 1823 on land leased from the Franciscans and demolished in 1883 to make way for the municipal theatre.
The Mercado de D. Pedro V in Funchal, built from 1876 with municipal loans and opened on 19 December 1880.
Survey of the ports and landing places of the Madeira archipelago, graded as good, tolerable or poor, with notes on recent improvements and a 1944 report on planned harbour works.

Former name of a large open space in Funchal, now the Campo do Almirante Reis, built in 1837 with proceeds from a student theatrical performance celebrating Queen Maria II's marriage. It was later landscaped and given a children's park, opened in 1939.
Lists the chapels in Madeira dedicated to Saint Anne (Santana), with their parishes, founders and dates of foundation where known, from 1607 to 1790.
The Boaventura stream, also called Ribeira de São Pedro, rises west of Pico das Abóboras in Santa Cruz municipality.
The Caniço stream rises at Camacha and receives the Vale Paraíso brook.
The Gonçalo Aires stream rises at Pico do Infante and carries little water.
The Santa Luzia stream, also called Ribeira da Praça, rises at Pico do Areeiro and Pico Escalvado.
The São João stream in Funchal rises at Pico Escalvado and Pico de Santo António and has borne many former names.
The Socorridos stream rises at the Torrinhas; its tributaries include the Ribeira de Vasco Gil.
The Vigário stream, also called Ribeira de Câmara de Lobos, rises at Achada do Poiso.
The Campanário stream, also called Ribeira da Lapa, rises at Pico dos Ferreiros and carries little water.
The Ribeira Brava stream rises at the São Vicente ridge; its tributaries are listed.
The Tabua stream rises at Pico das Pedras and receives the Barqueiro brook.

payload.name: Ribeira da Serra de Água da Calheta

own_entry.headword: Ribeira da Serra de Água da Calheta
own_entry.abstract: The Serra de Água stream of Calheta shares the Madalena stream's source and receives three brooks.
The Calheta stream rises at the Cabeço da Levadinha (Lombo do Salão) and receives the Cutileiro and Convento brooks.
The São Bartolomeu stream rises at Pico Gordo and Pico da Silva; its main tributary is the Farrobo brook.
A shoal near the bay of Câmara de Lobos.

Entry on the municipality of Câmara de Lobos, explaining that its seat was historically a 'lugar' rather than a vila, quoting Gaspar Frutuoso's description, and outlining the creation of the concelho in 1835 and later changes to its parishes.
A small coastal point in São Martinho parish, near the Gorgulho islet and Ponta da Cruz.
A 1,200-metre peak in the uplands of Calheta parish, near Monte das Estrebarias.

Summary entry listing the convents of the Franciscan order in Madeira: four friaries and three nunneries, most of them now gone. It also mentions the Jesuit college in Funchal, now used as a barracks.

Entry on the parish of Campanário, on Madeira's south coast west of Cabo Girão, explaining its name (from a bell-tower-shaped islet), its church history, early settlers, Jesuit estates and notable natives. It records the parish's move from Câmara de Lobos to the new Ribeira Brava municipality in 1914.

payload.name: Ilhéu, Porto e Ribeira de Porto da Cruz

own_entry.headword: Porto da Cruz (Ilhéu, Porto e Ribeira de)
own_entry.abstract: Short entry on three coastal features of Porto da Cruz parish that share its name: an islet, a small harbour whose landing place is called Furna, and a stream flowing into the sea nearby.
A 936 m peak between the parishes of Câmara de Lobos and Estreito, noted for its wide panoramic view.
A small hill about 100 m high in the parish of Campanário.
A 263 m coastal hill in São Martinho, formerly called Pico do Telégrafo, with fine views over Funchal and its bay.
One of the highest heights surrounding the parish of Serra de Água.
A headland in São Martinho regarded as the western limit of Funchal bay, once site of a small redoubt and near a fish-canning factory.
A small point on the northern coast of Porto Santo.
A stream rising at Pico da Pedreira and flowing between Ponta do Pargo and Achadas da Cruz to the sea near Fajã da Rocha.
Cape Cantim on the Moroccan coast, the African point at Madeira's latitude and closest to the archipelago, about 350 miles away.

A short entry on the valleys of Madeira, quoting a lyrical passage from the Diccionario Universal Ilustrado Portuguez that singles out the valleys of Machico, Funchal (with Vale Formoso), Jardim da Serra, São Vicente and Penha de Águia.
A 330 m peak overlooking Machico, once the site of a semaphore station, with a spring said to rise and fall with the tide.
The highest mountain on Porto Santo, in the north of the island, at 500 m.

payload.name: Capela do Sagrado Coração de Jesus

own_entry.abstract: Two chapels dedicated to the Sacred Heart of Jesus: one at Cardais, Água de Pena (1907), and one in Monte.

Entry on the parish of Santa Cruz, one of Madeira's oldest settlements, named after a cross Zarco had raised there at the discovery; it covers its early ecclesiastical history, collegiate church, chapels, noble settlers and localities.

payload.name: Ponta, Porto e Cais da Ponta do Sol

own_entry.headword: Ponta do Sol (Ponta, Porto e Cais da)
own_entry.abstract: Describes the headland, small harbour and quay of Ponta do Sol, on Madeira's south-west coast, and the possible origin of the name. The quay was built by the municipal council in 1848–1850; a later extension project of 1880 was never carried out.
Describes the relief of Porto Santo island: its hilly terrain, the main peaks with their heights, its two small plains and the chief headlands of its coast.

Describes the gates in Funchal's old city walls, listing those still standing in 1836 and when each was demolished, together with older references from 1597, King Sebastião's fortification regulations and Frutuoso.
Short account of the fort of Porto da Cruz, built in 1708 and dismantled in 1804, with a note on the Fort of Santo António at Paul do Mar, built in 1754.

payload.name: Forte de S. Jorge da Calheta

own_entry.headword: Forte de S. Jorge da Calheta
own_entry.abstract: Brief note on the Fort of São Jorge at Calheta, recording its captain in 1751.
Brief note on the redoubt in São Jorge parish, recording its captain in 1785.
The Fort of São Francisco in Santa Cruz, built in 1749 by order of the bishop-governor D. Fr. João do Nascimento and paid for with militia fines.

payload.name: Forte de S. José da Ilha do Porto Santo

own_entry.headword: Forte de S. José da Ilha do Porto Santo
own_entry.abstract: The Fort of São José in the town of Porto Santo, built under Pombal's government with a residence for the governors, and in 1921 ceded to the fiscal guard.
A small landing place on the coast of Seixal parish.

payload.name: Capelas de Nossa Senhora do Rosário

own_entry.abstract: Lists chapels dedicated to Our Lady of the Rosary in several Madeiran parishes, with their founders and dates of foundation.

payload.name: Capelas de Nossa Senhora da Salvação

own_entry.abstract: Describes two chapels of Our Lady of Salvation: a ruined one at Moinhos, Caniço, founded in 1614, and one in Funchal.

payload.name: Capela de Nossa Senhora da Saúde do Monte Olivete

own_entry.headword: Nossa Senhora da Saúde do Monte Olivete (Capela de)
own_entry.abstract: A vanished chapel in Santa Maria Maior, Funchal, built on an entail founded by Pedro Lopes de Vasconcelos in 1675.

payload.name: Capela de Nossa Senhora do Terço

own_entry.abstract: A chapel built by the people of Machico in 1770 beside the parish church.

payload.name: Capela de Nossa Senhora do Vale

own_entry.abstract: A chapel at Vale Formoso, Santa Luzia, founded and endowed by António Vogado in 1726.
The stream, also called Ribeira da Vila da Calheta, that flows into the town of Calheta, fed by several small tributaries.
Name given under D. Miguel to Funchal's Praça da Constituição, now part of Avenida Dr. Manuel de Arriaga, where troops paraded on feast days.

payload.name: Monumento a Nossa Senhora da Paz

own_entry.headword: Monumento a Nossa Senhora da Paz
own_entry.abstract: Marble statue of Our Lady of Peace with bronze reliefs and an adjoining chapel at the Terreiro da Luta, Monte, begun in 1923 and inaugurated in 1927 through the efforts of Father José Marques Jardim.

payload.name: Monumento ao Sagrado Coração de Jesus

own_entry.headword: Monumento ao Sagrado Coração de Jesus
own_entry.abstract: Statue of the Sacred Heart of Jesus erected by Aires de Ornelas de Vasconcelos at Ponta do Garajau, Caniço, blessed in 1927.
Bronze statue of João Gonçalves Zargo, first captain-donatary of Funchal, by Francisco Franco, inaugurated on the Avenida Arriaga in 1934.

payload.name: Monumento aos mortos da Grande Guerra

own_entry.headword: Monumento aos mortos da Grande Guerra
own_entry.abstract: Small memorial to those killed in the First World War, whose foundation stone was laid in Funchal in 1935.
Modest monument inaugurated in 1939 in the gardens of the Asilo de Mendicidade e Órfãos to Dr Alexandre da Cunha Teles, benefactor of charitable services.
Inhabited locality in Canhas parish, with a former chapel of 1733 and a recent chapel of the Sacred Heart.

History of the town and municipality of Calheta in western Madeira, created by royal charter of 1 July 1502, later seat of a countship granted to the captains of Funchal, and reorganised as a concelho in 1835.

Survey of the use of irrigation water in Madeira from settlement onwards, covering the building of levadas, the royal charters regulating water rights from the fifteenth century, and the State's later role in constructing levadas.
A belvedere at the Quinta das Angústias in Funchal, used as a landmark for anchoring, named after D. Guiomar Madalena Acciaioly, whose goods were seized for debts to the Treasury around 1800.

History of the São Lourenço Palace in Funchal, originally the fortress of São Lourenço, residence of the governors and military commanders of Madeira, with its successive alterations, chapel and state rooms.
Inhabited locality in Monte parish containing the Quinta da Paz with its chapel of Nossa Senhora do Livramento.
Pilgrims' shelters built at Monte, Santo António da Serra and Piedade on the Ponta de São Lourenço, with notes on their history.
Group of small islets and rocks off the coast of Faial parish, collectively known as the Ilhéus do Faial.
Stream rising near Pico Ruivo and reaching the sea at Faial, crossed by the longest bridge in Madeira, built 1907–1910.
Locality in Santa Maria Maior parish, Funchal, with the chapel of Nossa Senhora da Natividade founded by Zenobio Acciaioli in 1582.
Explains the Madeiran term fajã: fertile tracts formed by landslides, inland or along the coast, and a common place-name element.
Inhabited locality in Arco da Calheta parish, with ruins of a chapel of Nossa Senhora da Boa Hora.
Inhabited locality in Santo António parish on the left bank of the Ribeira dos Socorridos.

A Funchal street linking Rua dos Aranhas (now Dr. Chaves) with Largo do Ribeiro Real, opened when the old cemetery alleys were demolished. It is named after 5 June 1834, the date the constitutional government was proclaimed in Madeira.

A critical essay on the naming of streets in Funchal, recalling the municipal council's resolution of 19 June 1890 to name new streets after illustrious Madeirans and lamenting that it was seldom followed. It lists notable Madeirans still uncommemorated in 1921 and urges restraint in renaming old streets.
Former name (1896–1910) of the road between the parish church of Santo António and the Ribeira, honouring Luís de Bettencourt Miranda, long-serving secretary of the Funchal council.
Sub-entry of the Madeira survey on coastal hydrography, referring readers to the article on islets and listing the named reefs or shoals (baixas) around the Madeiran coast.

General description of the island of Porto Santo: its name, size, position, relief, beach, springs, administration and list of governors, settlement, vegetation, crops, geology and population. It stresses the island's poverty in water and its potential as a spa and bathing resort.
History of Funchal's fish market, the Praça do Peixe or Praça de São Pedro, from a small market built by the Câmara in 1817 to the building opened in 1840, later demolished for the Avenida do Mar.

The customs house of Machico, created by royal charter in 1477 alongside those of Funchal and Santa Cruz, was less busy than Santa Cruz's despite being at the captaincy seat. Its last Manueline ruins in Rua da Árvore were demolished in 1916.
The Fortress of São Lourenço in Funchal, begun under King Manuel I and completed under Philippine rule, was stormed by French pirates in 1566. It later housed a chapel and various public buildings.
Inhabited locality in the parish of Ribeira Brava, named after its chapel of São João Baptista, which was rebuilt in 1750.

History of the leper hospital of São Lázaro in Funchal, probably founded in the late 15th century, maintained by the Câmara, and closed in 1912, after which its building became the civil prison. It also records medical opinions on leprosy (elephantiasis) in Madeira.

The Teatro de Bom Gosto was a small theatre in Funchal, built around 1818–1820 near the Teatro Grande and owned by the first Count of Carvalhal, who had it refurbished after 1834. The last known performance there took place in 1838.
Entry on the town of Porto Santo (also called Baleira) as seat of a captaincy and a municipality, covering its lost foral and its nineteenth-century administrative reorganisation.
Describes the first dwellings built on Madeira after its discovery, made of local timber such as cedar, and records traditions about the first two-storey house and the first stone house in Funchal.

Describes two chapels dedicated to Saint Elizabeth: one inside the Misericórdia building in Funchal, probably built in the early eighteenth century and noted for its gilded carved altar, and another attached to the hospital of Santa Cruz.

payload.name: Colégio e Igreja de São João Evangelista

own_entry.headword: São João Evangelista (Colégio e Igreja de)
own_entry.abstract: History of the Jesuit college and church of São João Evangelista in Funchal, from the Jesuits' arrival in 1570 and the building's construction in the 17th century, through its later use as seminary, barracks and public offices, to the church's restoration in 1847. It also reproduces 18th-century descriptions of the chapels, their founders and benefactors.
Ilhéu Chão, the smallest and flattest of the Desertas, nearest to Ponta de São Lourenço.

The Quinta Lambert, or Quinta das Angústias, in Funchal was a celebrated estate whose house and chapel hosted royal visitors, including Queen Adelaide, the Duke of Leuchtenberg and the Empress Amélia of Brazil, whose daughter Princess Maria Amélia died there in 1853. The estate was bought by Dr Júlio Paulo de Freitas in 1903.

Survey of places and buildings in Madeira regarded as 'memorable landmarks' of Portuguese discovery and settlement: the island itself, the Desembarcadouro at Machico, the Santa Catarina chapel, Santa Clara church, the Quinta das Cruzes and the Senhor dos Milagres chapel at Machico.
Ponta do Pargo is the rugged headland forming Madeira's westernmost point, site of the lighthouse.

payload.name: Rua da Princesa D. Maria Amelia

own_entry.abstract: Funchal street named by the municipal council in 1852 to mark Princess Maria Amélia's visit to Madeira. It links Rua da Imperatriz D. Amélia with the area near the Pontinha.

History of the town and municipality of São Vicente on Madeira's north coast, raised to a town (vila) by royal charter in 1744 to free northern parishes from distant Machico, and reorganised as a municipality in 1835. It also covers later boundary changes involving Porto Moniz and plans to move the municipal seat.

Public park at Monte, above Funchal, begun by the municipal council in 1894 and named after council president Dr José Leite Monteiro; it contains the marble Fonte de Nossa Senhora with an 18th-century inscription recording Charles Murray's purchase of its water.

payload.name: Castelo de S. João do Pico

own_entry.abstract: The Castle of São João do Pico is a fortress on the Pico dos Frias, north-west of and overlooking Funchal and its harbour. According to the Elucidário it was built between 1622 and 1640, and it later served for a time as the district prison.

Entry on the small north-coast parish of Arco de São Jorge, between São Jorge and Boaventura, created in 1676. It covers its church history, fertility and climate, the remarkable landslide of 1689 that formed the Quebrada, and notable natives.

The Fortress of São Tiago, built on a rocky point east of Funchal harbour during the Philippine period (dated 1614), was later enlarged and rebuilt in 1767. It housed British gunners during the English occupation and, in 1921, a mountain artillery battery.
Aviceiro, or Fonte do Aviceiro, is a locality in the parish of Santo António, near Lombo de D. Isabel. It lies on the road leading to Curral das Freiras.

payload.name: Avenida do Doutor Jose Antonio de Almada

own_entry.headword: Doutor Jose Antonio de Almada (Avenida do)
own_entry.abstract: Avenue in Funchal named after Dr José António de Almada, formerly the Pontinha road, built around 1874 along the coast south of the Vigias and Lambert quintas.

payload.name: Albergaria e Capela de S. Bartolomeu

own_entry.headword: Albergaria e Capela de S. Bartolomeu
own_entry.abstract: A hostel for poor clergy with an adjoining chapel of São Bartolomeu in Funchal, founded by Gonçalo Anes de Velosa in 1497; the first Jesuits lodged there before their college was founded.

A populated locality in the parish of Ponta do Sol, named after its chapel of São João, an entailed property of the Berenguer de França family whose head took the title of viscount of São João from the place.
